lessons.title: die Uhr — "the clock"
lessons.gloss: the clock, and o'clock — the first everyday German word in this book that Rome supplied

segments.text: Something changes here. The numbers were German's own and the weekdays were German's gods — this word is neither.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: die Uhr

segments.text: die Uhr — "the clock," and also "o'clock."
A die-word, and one syllable. It does two jobs: the object on the wall, and the word you say when telling the time.
u-long — a long u, the vowel of English moor.
r-final — and then a soft r that barely closes: German's final r colours the vowel and stops rather than rolling.
Together: oor. One syllable, nothing more.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: its two jobs — "the clock; o'clock"]

segments.instruction: it beside a word you own — "der Tag, die Uhr"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it beside a word you own — "der Tag, die Uhr"]

segments.text: "die Uhr."

Say "the clock." (Die Uhr.) Which article? (Die.) How many syllables? (One — oor.) What else does the word mean? (O'clock.) Next: where it came from, which is not where the rest of this book's words come from.

lessons.title: Uhr, taken apart
lessons.gloss: the third layer of the German day — numbers native, weekdays Germanic, the clock Latin

segments.text: You have twice met a language keeping some words and buying others. Here is the third time, and it completes a picture.
Uhr comes from Latin hōra, "hour" — the same word that became French heure, Italian ora and English hour. It reached German through medieval Latin and Low German ūr(e).
Timekeeping arrived with Roman and monastic clocks, and the word rode in with the machinery.
Three layers of the German day, three different origins:

utterances: what: the numbers. German: eins, zwei, drei. where it came from: native Germanic.
what: the weekdays. German: Montag, Donnerstag. where it came from: Germanic gods.
what: the clock. German: Uhr. where it came from: Latin, from hōra.

segments.text: German kept its own counting and its own gods. For the machine that measures hours it reached for Rome.

That is the same rule you were given with the months and again with Samstag: the words used every hour of every day are the hardest to displace, and the words that arrive with an institution come in whole. A clock is an institution arriving.

segments.text: "Uhr — from hōra."

Which Latin word is Uhr? (Hōra.) Which English word is its cousin? (Hour.) Which two layers of the German day are not borrowed? (The numbers and the weekdays.) Why did this one come in? (It arrived with the clocks.) Next: the German word that was there already.

lessons.title: die Stunde — "an hour"
lessons.gloss: an hour's span — the native word that survived beside the borrowed one, with the jobs divided

segments.text: A borrowed word usually arrives because a language needs one. This time German already had a perfectly good word, and took the Latin one anyway.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: die Stunde

segments.text: die Stunde — "an hour," in the sense of a span of sixty minutes.
Native Germanic, and older in the language than Uhr. It is the word for a duration: a lesson lasts eine Stunde.
st-initial-scht — a German st- at the start of a word is sht-, not st-. So this opens SHTOON-, which is the single most useful spelling rule in German after ei and ie.
u-long — the same long u you met in Uhr.
The loan did not push the native word out. The two divided the work instead:

utterances: for: reading a clock — "o'clock". German uses: Uhr.
for: a length of time — "an hour". German uses: Stunde.

segments.text: English has the same split and hides it: hour covers both, and o'clock is a worn-down phrase (of the clock) doing the first job.
This is worth holding on to, because it is what borrowing usually looks like. The loan rarely kills the native word; it takes a slice of the meaning and the two settle into different rooms.

segments.instruction: the pair and their jobs — "Uhr for the clock, Stunde for the span"

segments.text: "die Uhr, die Stunde."

Say "an hour," meaning a span. (Eine Stunde.) Which word do you use to read a clock? (Uhr.) Which of the two is native German? (Stunde.) How is st- pronounced at the start of a word? (Sht-.) Next: putting Uhr into a sentence.

lessons.title: Es ist zwei Uhr — telling the time
lessons.gloss: telling the time — es ist, a number you own, and Uhr

segments.text: You have the numbers and you have the word. The frame that joins them needs nothing new.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: es ist, a number, Uhr

segments.text: es ist + the number + Uhr.
Es ist ein Uhr. — "It is one o'clock." Es ist zwei Uhr. — "It is two o'clock." Es ist zehn Uhr. — "It is ten o'clock."
Word for word that is the English sentence with o'clock moved: it is two o'clock. Nothing about the order has to be relearned.
One thing to notice: at one o'clock it is ein Uhr, not eins — the counting form drops its -s here exactly as it does before a noun, which you met with ein and eine.

segments.instruction: "Es ist zwei Uhr." "Es ist zehn Uhr."
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Es ist zwei Uhr." "Es ist zehn Uhr."]

segments.instruction: the odd one — "Es ist ein Uhr", not eins
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the odd one — "Es ist ein Uhr", not *eins*]

segments.instruction: the hour it is now, wherever you are
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the hour it is now, wherever you are]

segments.text: "Es ist zwei Uhr."

Say "it is ten o'clock." (Es ist zehn Uhr.) What are the three pieces? (Es ist, the number, Uhr.) What happens to eins at one o'clock? (It drops the -s: ein Uhr.) Next: the plural German does not use here.

lessons.title: zwei Uhr, not zwei Uhren
lessons.gloss: Uhr takes no plural when it means o'clock — it works like English o'clock, not like clocks

segments.text: Every German noun you have met takes a plural. This one refuses — but only in one of its two jobs.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the clock-reading Uhr does not count

segments.text: Telling the time, Uhr stays singular however many hours you name.
Zwei Uhr is "two o'clock." Not zwei Uhren — that would be two clocks, the objects on the wall.

English does the identical thing and hides it behind an apostrophe. You would never say "two o'clocks" either, because o'clock is not a noun being counted — it is a fossilised phrase, of the clock. German's Uhr is doing that job with no apostrophe to warn you.

So what you are watching is not really about Uhr. It is about a word that has stopped being a countable thing and become a unit of time, a job nouns take on in every language and mark differently in each.

segments.instruction: the English that hides it — "two o'clock, two clocks"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the English that hides it — "two o'clock, two clocks"]

segments.text: "zwei Uhr; zwei Uhren."

Say "two o'clock." (Zwei Uhr.) Say "two clocks." (Zwei Uhren.) Which of the two is the plural? (Uhren.) Why does the time not take one? (It is a unit of time, not a thing being counted.) Next: the two pivots of the day, and they are German's own.

lessons.title: die Mitte — "the middle"
lessons.gloss: the middle — the native piece both of the day's pivots are built from

segments.text: The clock-word was Latin. The two pivots of the German day swing straight back to German's own vocabulary, and they share a piece.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: die Mitte

segments.text: die Mitte — "the middle."
Two syllables, short i, and a crisp doubled t: MIT-tuh.
Mitte is English mid and middle — the same inherited word, and you can hear it without being told.
Its Latin cousin is medius, "middle," which English borrowed several times over: medium, median, mediocre (literally "middling"), and the medi- of Mediterranean, the sea in the middle of the land.

So the everyday Germanic word and the learned Latin one sit side by side in English, and German has the first of them. That is the pattern you have been watching all book: two doors into one root, one worn smooth by daily use and one carried in by scholars.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the Germanic side — "Mitte, mid, middle"]
[YOU SAY: the Latin side — "medius, medium, median"]

segments.text: "die Mitte — the middle."

Say "the middle." (Die Mitte.) Which two English words is it? (Mid and middle.) Which Latin word is its cousin? (Medius.) Name an English word from that side. (Medium, median or mediocre.) Next: the middle of the day.

lessons.title: der Mittag — "noon"
lessons.gloss: noon — Mitte plus Tag, a compound you can read before you are told it

segments.text: You have the middle and you have the day. Put them together before reading on — you will be right.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Mittag

segments.text: der Mittag — "noon," and literally "mid-day."
Mitt- from Mitte, -tag from Tag. Nothing is hidden and nothing had to be learned: this is the third compound in two chapters you could read on sight, after Montag and Sonnabend.
English has the identical compound — midday — built from the identical two inherited words. Neither language got it from the other; each still had the pieces and used them.
To say it is noon: Es ist Mittag. No number and no Uhr, because noon is not an hour you count to.
"der Mittag — midday."
Say "noon." (Der Mittag.) What are its two pieces? (Mitte and Tag.) Say "it is noon." (Es ist Mittag.) Does it need a number? (No.) Next: what French does with the same idea, and why German did not.

lessons.title: Mittag and midi
lessons.gloss: German and French mean the same thing by noon — but German built it and French inherited it

segments.text: French says midi for noon, and it means exactly what Mittag means. That is not a borrowing in either direction.
French midi comes from Latin medius diēs — "middle day." German Mittag is Mitte plus Tag — "middle day."
The same thought, assembled twice, out of different material:

utterances: language: Latin, then French. built from: medius + diēs. result: midi.
language: German. built from: Mitte + Tag. result: Mittag.

segments.text: Both families looked at the sun overhead and named the moment for the middle of the day. Neither copied the other; the idea is obvious enough that two languages reached it independently, and each used the words it had.
This is the counterweight to Uhr, and the two are worth holding together.
For the clock — a machine that arrived from outside — German took the foreign word whole. For noon — something anyone with a sky already has — German built its own out of pieces it owned.
A language borrows what arrives and builds what was always there. One chapter, both halves of that.

segments.instruction: what each is made of — "Mitte plus Tag; medius plus diēs"

segments.text: "Mittag, midi — the same thought, built twice."

What is French midi made of? (Medius + diēs, "middle day".) And Mittag? (Mitte + Tag.) Did German borrow it? (No — it built its own.) Which word in this chapter was borrowed? (Uhr.) Next: the other pivot.

lessons.title: die Mitternacht — "midnight"
lessons.gloss: midnight — the second pivot, and the -cht/-ght pair paying off again

segments.text: The day's other pivot, and the second compound in this chapter you can assemble from words you already have.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: die Mitternacht

segments.text: die Mitternacht — "midnight," literally "mid-night."
Mitter- is Mitte with the linking form it takes inside a compound, and -nacht is the night. English midnight is the same two words again.
To say it: Es ist Mitternacht. Like Mittag, no number and no Uhr.
ch-ach — the raspy back-of-the-throat sound from Nacht itself, unchanged inside the longer word.
And that -cht is the correspondence you were given with the numbers: German -cht- answers English -ght- every time.
You met the first pair counting to ten. Here it is again on a word you now need, which is what a sound correspondence is for — you learn it once and it keeps paying.
"Mittag, Mitternacht."

Say "midnight." (Die Mitternacht.) What are its pieces? (Mitte and Nacht.) What does German -cht- answer in English? (-ght-.) Give the pair you met with the numbers. (Acht / eight.) Next: the whole chapter, said through.

lessons.title: Practice — the clock and the two pivots
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — the borrowed clock and the two native pivots, said together

segments.text: No new words. One borrowed word and two built ones, and the difference between them is the chapter. Start by saying the borrowed one, one long syllable — Uhr — and then the piece both pivots begin with, Mitte.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three ways to say when

utterances: when: one o'clock. German: Es ist ein Uhr.
when: ten o'clock. German: Es ist zehn Uhr.
when: noon. German: Es ist Mittag.
when: midnight. German: Es ist Mitternacht.

segments.text: One frame, es ist, and then either a number with Uhr or a pivot on its own. The pivots take no number because they are not hours you count to.
Hold the two halves of the chapter side by side:
Uhr came from Latin hōra, with the clocks. German had Stunde already, so the loan took the clock-reading job and the native word kept the span.
Mittag and Mitternacht are German's own, built from Mitte with Tag and Nacht — the same thought French assembled out of Latin as midi.
A language borrows what arrives and builds what was always there. The sky was always there; the clock was delivered.
